findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement forecast to rise 31% from £21.7m to £28.4m by 2029; council shifting to net borrower status
findings.detail: Liability Benchmark shows CFR growing from £21.7m (2026 actual) to £28.4m (2029 forecast). Asset Benchmark indicates council will shift from current net investment position of £32.5m to requiring £10.1m external borrowing by 2029, representing a significant rebalancing of the debt portfolio.
findings.matters: Material increase in planned capital spending and borrowing requirements signals a shift in council's financial strategy; affects debt sustainability, refinancing requirements, and medium-term funding dependency.
findings.figures: CFR forecast: £21.7m (2026), £25.3m (2027), £27.7m (2028), £28.4m (2029); Asset Benchmark: £10.1m external borrowing required by 2029
findings.quote: The liability benchmark is an important tool to help establish whether the Council is likely to be a long-term borrower or long-term investor in the future, and so shape its strategic focus and decision making.

findings.headline: £8m short-term loans borrowed at year-end to support cash flow; represents 75% of total borrowing
findings.detail: Council took £8m in short-term loans at year-end which matured in April 2026 to manage cash flow. This increased total borrowing from £2.8m to £10.7m. The scale of this borrowing relative to total debt and its short-term nature suggests material cash timing challenges.
findings.matters: Substantial reliance on short-term borrowing for cash management indicates underlying revenue/expenditure timing mismatches; creates refinancing risk and dependence on short-term market conditions.
findings.figures: £8m short-term loans at year-end; total borrowing increased from £2.8m to £10.7m (£8.2m short-term, £2.5m long-term)
findings.quote: Short Term Loans totalling £8m were taken out at year end to support cash flow, and matured in April 2026.

findings.headline: Usable reserves fell by £4.7m to £33.6m; working capital down £6.7m amid volatile cash flows
findings.detail: Usable reserves declined from £38.3m to £33.6m. Working capital fell from £15.9m to £9.2m. Investment balances ranged between £58.0m and £29.3m during the year, indicating material cash flow volatility and a tighter overall liquidity position.
findings.matters: Declining reserves and tight working capital reduce financial flexibility. The wide swing in investment balances (£29m range) indicates the council operates with compressed cash buffers and requires careful cash flow management.
findings.figures: Reserves £33.6m (down £4.7m from 2025); working capital £9.2m (down £6.7m); investment range £58.0m to £29.3m
findings.quote: During the year, the Authority's investment balances ranged between £58.0m and £29.3m due to timing differences between income and expenditure.

findings.headline: Council temporarily exceeded Money Market Fund counterparty limit due to administrative error
findings.detail: During 2025/26, the council exceeded the approved counterparty limit for one Money Market Fund. The breach was identified through routine monitoring and rectified promptly with no financial loss. The investment remained within an approved category and processes were reviewed to prevent recurrence.
findings.matters: Even though minor and quickly fixed, the breach indicates a control weakness in counterparty management; relevant to assessing governance and internal control quality.
findings.figures: One temporary breach; no financial loss; investment remained approved
findings.quote: During the year, the council temporarily exceeded the approved counterparty limit for one Money Market Fund due to an administrative error. The breach was identified through routine monitoring and rectified promptly.

findings.headline: Accounts Receivable / Debt Management audit concluded with Limited assurance opinion
findings.detail: The audit of Accounts Receivable and Debt Management reached reporting stage with a Limited assurance conclusion. Limited assurance indicates that auditors identified control weaknesses or inconsistent control application that could affect the council's ability to manage its debt collection and receivables effectively.
findings.matters: Lenders and the s151 officer need to understand control gaps in debt management, as this directly affects the council's ability to collect income owed to it and maintain cash flow. This is a material audit weakness in a core financial function.
findings.figures: Limited assurance (rated outcome for one of 18% of planned audits reaching reporting stage)
findings.quote: The audit of Accounts Receivable / Debt Management has concluded with a 'Limited' assurance opinion

findings.headline: Internal audit plan delivery is severely behind schedule: only 18% complete against a 90% target, with 33% of audits meeting timescales against an 80% target.
findings.detail: Performance data shows the audit function is delivering well below targets for plan completion and timeliness. Only 18% of the agreed annual audit plan has been completed (draft or final reports issued) by July, against a target of 90% and a typical expectation of 60% by mid-year.
findings.matters: Slow audit delivery means governance weaknesses are not being identified and reported promptly. This is a leading indicator that control assurance is behind.
findings.figures: 18% plan completion (target 90%); 33% on-time delivery for draft reports (target 80%)
findings.quote: Percentage of the agreed audit plan completed (issue of draft / final report) Ongoing 90% 18%

findings.headline: Multiple audit actions across different areas are overdue and being retired rather than completed, indicating governance follow-up is not happening.
findings.detail: Four medium-priority actions are overdue (from HR, Tree Management, and Safeguarding audits). Two overdue actions from a 2022 Lease Income audit will not be implemented as intended and are being retired. One overdue action from the July 2025 Accounts Receivable audit has also been retired rather than completed.
findings.matters: Retiring actions rather than completing them indicates the council is not addressing identified control weaknesses. This suggests governance and oversight of audit follow-up is weak.
findings.figures: 4 overdue medium-priority actions; 2 actions retired from 2022; 1 action retired from July 2025
findings.quote: The management team have also provided confirmation that two overdue actions in respect of Lease Income and Asset Management (Tenanted Properties) – finalised November 2022, will no longer be implemented as originally intended and are therefore considered 'retired'.

findings.headline: Accounts Receivable audit receives 'Limited' assurance opinion (the second-worst rating), requiring corrective actions by end of October 2026.
findings.detail: The Accounts Receivable/Debt Management audit concluded with a Limited opinion, indicating significant gaps and weaknesses in controls. Five medium-priority and one low-priority management actions were agreed, with corrective action deadlines extending to the end of October 2026.
findings.matters: Limited assurance means controls are not adequate to manage risks. This is the second system implementation of receivables controls in two years (the July 2025 audit also had issues), indicating persistent control weakness.
findings.figures: 5 medium and 1 low priority actions; implementation by end October 2026
findings.quote: To address the issues identified, appropriate, corrective actions have been agreed for implementation during quarter two 2026 with the final action due by the end of October 2026.

findings.headline: The Accounts Receivable control account cannot reconcile to the General Ledger, and has been failing since the TechnologyOne system went live.
findings.detail: The audit was unable to test GL reconciliation and no evidence was provided that this reconciliation had been performed. Finance staff advised this reconciliation has been unsuccessful throughout 2025-26 due to an issue with TechnologyOne.
findings.matters: Inability to reconcile the AR subledger to GL means the council's financial statements cannot be verified as accurate. This is a fundamental accounting control failure.
findings.figures: Failed reconciliation throughout 2025-26 (12 months)
findings.quote: We were unable to test whether the Accounts Receivable control account reconciles to the General Ledger, and no evidence was provided that this had been successfully performed by the Finance Team. We were advised that this had been unsuccessful throughout 2025-26 due to an issue with the TechnologyOne system.

findings.headline: Debt recovery process has been suspended since the new finance system went live in April 2025, with no reminder letters issued and no formal recovery action in place.
findings.detail: The TechnologyOne system has not been configured to issue automatic reminder letters to debtors. Manual letters were not issued either. The Debt Management Policy prescribes three stages of reminder letters, but the audit found no recovery action occurs. This means all debts have effectively been suspended pending a formal recovery process.
findings.matters: Unable to collect outstanding receivables is a cash flow and liquidity risk to the council. No KPIs are currently being monitored to track collection performance despite the policy requiring this.
findings.figures: 0 reminder letters issued since April 2025 go-live; 0 KPIs being measured or monitored despite policy requiring two
findings.quote: The audit confirmed, however, that since the go-live of the new TechnologyOne system in April 2025, no reminder letters have been issued to any debtors... in reality, all debts have effectively been suspended until there is a formalised/scheduled recovery process in place.

findings.headline: Audit fee variation required; scope of work increased beyond scale fee.
findings.detail: The risk assessment procedures, MHCLG submission, and rebuilding of historic assurance are all outside the scale fee. EY will seek variation once costs are agreed.
findings.matters: Additional audit costs and extended engagement signal unplanned scope increase and resource impact on council.
findings.figures: None specified
findings.quote: the activities undertaken in relation to this risk assessment, the preparation of the submission required by MHCLG, and the drafting of this addendum are outside the scope of the scale fee set out in our Audit Planning Report issued on 27 April 2026. In addition, procedures relating to the rebuilding of historical assurance will also be outside the scale fee. Accordingly, we will seek a variation to the scale fee

findings.headline: Council must demonstrate sufficient finance capacity to support historic reserve rebuild without compromising current-year audit.
findings.detail: EY explicitly requires the council to confirm it has capacity to provide high-quality working papers and support the rebuilding of historic assurance over 2022/23 transactions while delivering planned 2025/26 audit procedures. Management must complete robust review and reconciliation of all reserves.
findings.matters: EY's explicit capacity concern indicates potential resource constraints in the finance team. Insufficient capacity to handle both historic rebuild and current audit is a control environment weakness.
findings.figures: Work extends back to 2022/23
findings.quote: we will require confirmation that high-quality working papers and supporting evidence can be provided, together with sufficient management capacity to support this historic rebuild without compromising the delivery of planned audit procedures for 2025/26 over closing balances and in-year movements.

findings.headline: Audit opinion will remain qualified in 2025/26; unqualified status unlikely before 2026/27 at earliest.
findings.detail: EY's timeline shows the council will progress from disclaimed to qualified opinion at best in 2025/26. PPE valuation timing means that even after completing 2025/26 audit, issues with 2024/25 comparatives will continue to impact the audit opinion.
findings.matters: A continued qualified opinion signals unresolved control or accounting issues persisting into the next cycle. Lenders require clean audit opinions.
findings.figures: Timeline extends to 2026/27 for potential unqualified opinion
findings.quote: We will not, however, have assurance over associated movements in income and expenditure in 2025/26 and the valuation of that PPE in the 2024/25 comparative year. This will therefore continue to impact the form of the opinion we are able to issue.

findings.headline: Capital Adjustment Account presents management bias risk affecting reported General Fund balance.
findings.detail: EY identifies that adjustments between the Capital Adjustment Account and General Fund directly influence reported General Fund balance, creating potential for management to misstate capital entries to present a stronger revenue position.
findings.matters: This describes a control weakness where management incentive exists to manipulate capital accounting to artificially improve the General Fund balance and reported financial resilience.
findings.figures: None specified
findings.quote: The Capital Adjustment Account has some susceptibility to misstatement due to management bias, as adjustments made between the CAA and the General Fund directly influence the reported General Fund balance. This creates a potential incentive to misstate or inappropriately adjust capital entries in order to present a stronger revenue position or higher level of financial resilience.

findings.headline: General Fund Balance carries material unaudited movements and is unassured.
findings.detail: The General Fund (the key indicator of financial resilience) has been assessed as higher inherent risk due to sensitivity to accounting adjustments and material movements during the disclaimed period. This reserve remains unaudited.
findings.matters: The General Fund shows the council's actual financial flexibility and sustainability. Without audit assurance, stated reserves position and financial resilience cannot be trusted.
findings.figures: Assessed as higher inherent risk
findings.quote: The General Fund has been assessed as a higher inherent risk due to its sensitivity to statutory accounting adjustments and its role as a key indicator of financial resilience, with material unaudited movements identified in the disclaimed period.

findings.headline: Two consecutive years of disclaimed audit opinions on the accounts.
findings.detail: The council's 2023/24 and 2024/25 accounts received no audit opinion due to unresolved issues over PPE valuations from 2022/23, total reserves classification, grants received in advance, and IFRS 16 lease recognition. The financial statements cannot be assured.
findings.matters: A disclaimed opinion means the auditor cannot verify the council's financial position. For lenders, this creates uncertainty about reported reserves and resilience.
findings.figures: Two financial years (2023/24, 2024/25) affected
findings.quote: In 2023/24 and 2024/25, a disclaimer of opinion was issued due to the application of the backstop and lack of assurance over: the valuation of land and buildings included within property, plant and equipment that were revalued in 2022/23 and the consequential impact of these on the Comprehensive Income and Expenditure Statement; the total of reserves and their classification

findings.headline: Assurance over historic reserve balances will need to be rebuilt over future audit cycles
findings.detail: Management must complete robust reviews and reconciliations and provide high-quality working papers and evidence to support the 2025/26 audit. The rebuild of assurance will extend across multiple future audit cycles—this is not a one-year fix.
findings.matters: The council will not achieve an unmodified audit opinion in 2025/26; this is a multi-year recovery process during which reserve balances remain uncertain
findings.figures: Multiple audit cycles required
findings.quote: assurance over historic reserve balances will need to be rebuilt over future audit cycles, with management required to complete robust reviews and reconciliations and provide high-quality working papers and evidence to support the 2025/26 audit.

findings.headline: Reserve balances may include cumulative effect of unaudited transactions over more than one financial year
findings.detail: The National Audit Office's Local Authority Reset and Recovery guidance requires auditors to assess areas where audit risk may have accumulated over disclaimed periods. The council's reserves may contain multiple years of unaudited activity embedded in their balances.
findings.matters: Multiple years of unaudited transactions mean the true composition and accuracy of reserve balances is fundamentally unknown
findings.figures: More than one financial year of potentially unaudited activity
findings.quote: risk assessment procedures over reserves because these balances may include the cumulative effect of unaudited transactions over more than one financial year.

findings.headline: General Fund Balance, Capital Grants Unapplied Account, Revaluation Reserve and Capital Adjustment Account assessed as higher inherent risk
findings.detail: EY identified these four key reserves as carrying higher inherent risk due to scale of movements, accounting complexity, judgement involved and potential impact on the reported financial position. The General Fund Balance—the council's main financial cushion—is among the uncertain balances.
findings.matters: If the General Fund Balance and other major reserves are uncertain, the council's actual liquidity and financial standing is unknown to lenders
findings.figures: Four named reserves flagged as higher risk
findings.quote: some balances, including the General Fund Balance, Capital Grants Unapplied Account, Revaluation Reserve and Capital Adjustment Account, carry a higher inherent risk due to the scale of movements, accounting complexity, judgement involved and potential impact on the reported financial position.

findings.headline: Council received disclaimed audit opinions for 2023/24 and 2024/25 due to insufficient assurance over reserve balances
findings.detail: EY could not express an audit opinion on Havant's accounts for two consecutive years, reflecting the absence of sufficient assurance over a number of balances including reserves and their classification. This is a fundamental audit failure.
findings.matters: Disclaimed audit opinions mean the council's financial accounts remain unaudited and unverified—a critical governance failure that directly affects a lender's ability to assess the council's financial position
findings.quote: The Council received disclaimed audit opinions for 2023/24 and 2024/25, reflecting the application of statutory backstop arrangements and the absence of sufficient assurance over a number of balances, including reserves and their classification.

findings.headline: Major cyber-attack risk escalated to 16 following actual bot attacks in March 2026
findings.detail: Two bot attacks in quick succession in March 2026 overloaded the website search function, causing timeouts and error messages. The risk score increased from 12 to 16 post-mitigation as likelihood rose from 3 to 4 (impact unchanged at 4). The council installed Turnstile protection on the search function; no further attacks have occurred.
findings.matters: Demonstrated cyber vulnerability and escalated risk level indicate potential for operational disruption affecting service delivery and council operations
findings.figures: Score increased from 12 to 16; likelihood from 3 to 4
findings.quote: HB003 - Major cyber-attack on the Council or a Council supplier has increased from 12 to 16 after mitigation. This reflects an increase in likelihood from 3 to 4, while impact remains at 4, following two bot attacks in quick succession in March 2026.

findings.headline: Council has identified potential excessive financial burdens as a corporate-level risk above acceptable threshold
findings.detail: Havant identifies this as one of three corporate risks scoring 16 or above post-mitigation (the acceptable threshold). This is subject to quarterly review and updated mitigations. The council states that all proposed mitigating actions can be accommodated within existing budgets.
findings.matters: Explicit identification of financial burden risks at corporate level suggests material structural challenges that would be relevant to lending decisions
findings.figures: Post-mitigation score of 16 or above
findings.quote: Currently there are three corporate risks scoring above the acceptable risk threshold (a post-mitigation of score of 16 or above). • Potential excessive financial burdens affecting the authority

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation creates resource pressures during a compressed 22-month transition to vesting day April 2028
findings.detail: Following the government decision in March 2026, Havant is delivering LGR across Hampshire with a Shadow Authority in place by May 2027 and a new unitary authority taking over services 1 April 2028. The register identifies significant resource requirements in HR, Property, and Finance to deliver this transformation while maintaining existing priorities. A July 2026 note flags that this risk needs close monitoring through to vesting day.
findings.matters: Compressed timelines and dual-running costs during LGR create cashflow pressure and delivery risk; governance disruption during transition period compounds financial management challenges.
findings.figures: Shadow Authority in place by May 2027; vesting day 1 April 2028; significant work required in HR, Property, Finance
findings.quote: Significant work required in HR, Property, Finance to ensure the organisation is able to deliver LGR in a timely way whilst still delivering priorities. July 26 - Given Vesting Day is April 2028 this risk needs to be closely monitored

findings.headline: £1.7m savings programme underway but three-year funding settlement declines in years two and three
findings.detail: The council has agreed a £1.7m savings and efficiency programme and agreed budget for 2026/27, and the Fair Funding Review delivered a three-year funding settlement starting April 2026. However, the register explicitly warns that while the funding position improves in year one (2026/27), it reduces in years two and three. Simultaneously, Local Government Reorganisation is creating crystallising financial challenges that require close recognition.
findings.matters: A frontloaded funding settlement with declining support creates a medium-term affordability cliff; combined with LGR transition costs, the council will face mounting pressure after 2026/27 to sustain services or find further savings.
findings.figures: £1.7m savings programme; three-year settlement from April 2026 with declining funding in years 2 and 3
findings.quote: Savings and Efficiency Programme agreed (£1.7m) and budget for 2026/27 agreed and being implemented. Fair Funding Review resulted in new three year funding settlement beginning in April 2026. Improved funding position in 2026/27 but funding reduces in years two and three. Local Government Reorganisation decision made and work now at pace. Financial challenges starting to crystalise and scale of financial risk needs to be recognised.

findings.headline: A £49m remediation liability for coastal pollution on council-owned land
findings.detail: The register identifies a significant contingent liability from potential clean-up and remediation of pollution spills from council-owned land into environmentally designated areas. The council estimates this at £49m and notes potential for environmental fines from regulators. This appears in the Failing Coastal Assets risk (HB014). The risk score has improved from 20 to 9 post-mitigation through investment in coastal schemes and the Hayling Island Strategy, but the scale of the underlying liability remains material.
findings.matters: A £49m liability represents a material claim on council reserves or future cashflow and creates regulatory exposure; critical for lenders assessing balance sheet risk and financial flexibility.
findings.figures: £49m estimated remediation and clean-up cost; potential environmental fines
findings.quote: Potential clean up and remediation for pollution spill from Council owned land into environmentally designated areas are estimated in the order of £49m with potential for environmental fines.

findings.paper_title: Report - Revenue, Capital and Prudential Indicators Outturn Reports 202526
findings.headline: £191k provision for accrued interest liabilities on Section 106 developer contributions indicates delays in deploying capital contributions
findings.detail: The council has recognised a £191k provision for interest liabilities associated with Section 106 developer contributions. Interest continues to accrue on unspent balances until the contributions are applied for their specified purposes. This suggests developer contributions are not being deployed on schedule.
findings.matters: Unspent developer contributions with accruing interest create unbudgeted costs and signal delays in capital project delivery or deployment.
findings.figures: £191k provision for s106 interest liability in 2025/26
findings.quote: A provision of £191k has been recognised within the 2025/26 accounts in respect of potential interest liabilities associated with certain s106 developer contributions. Under the terms of the relevant agreements, interest continues to accrue on unspent balances until the contributions are applied for their specified purposes.

findings.paper_title: Report - Revenue, Capital and Prudential Indicators Outturn Reports 202526
findings.headline: Housing funding model gap: local government funding did not recognize demand-led housing pressures until 2026/27
findings.detail: The S151 Officer notes that continued demand-led pressure from housing services was not recognised in the local government funding model until 2026/27, creating a structural lag. The service baseline budget has been uplifted for 2026/27 to recognise the rise in demand, but the ongoing national housing crisis remains a significant risk outside the council's control.
findings.matters: This indicates a systemic mismatch between demand and funding allocation; the 2026/27 uplift may prove insufficient if demand continues to grow, risking further reserves drawdown.
findings.figures: Housing Service baseline budget uplift in 2026/27; ongoing national housing crisis cited as significant risk
findings.quote: Continued demand led pressure from on the Housing services have not been recognised in the local government funding model until 2026/27. Furthermore, initiatives to reduce the cost of provision have seen delays. These pressures have been mitigated somewhat by investment in early intervention and prevention, yet the Housing services remain the key driver of the Council's operational overspend.

findings.paper_title: Report - Revenue, Capital and Prudential Indicators Outturn Reports 202526
findings.headline: £13.3m (53%) of the capital programme was reprofiled into future years due to delivery delays and slippage
findings.detail: The capital programme delivered £11.8m against a revised budget of £25.1m. Major slippage occurred in the Housing portfolio (Waterlooville Leisure Centre, housing purchase programme) and Commercial portfolio (Food Waste programme impacted by national procurement challenges). The council has created a Major Projects Board to monitor and reduce future slippage.
findings.matters: Capital slippage over 50% signals project delivery risk and planning weaknesses; the council's recent creation of a Major Projects Board to oversee delivery suggests prior governance issues.
findings.figures: £11.8m expenditure against £25.1m revised budget; £13.3m slippage (53%) reprofiled to 2026/27
findings.quote: The 2025/26 capital outturn was £11.8m against a £25.1m programme, resulting in £13.3m slippage into 2026/27. The slippage was primarily driven by delays within the Housing portfolio.

findings.paper_title: Report - Revenue, Capital and Prudential Indicators Outturn Reports 202526
findings.headline: Housing Service £2.3m overspend from temporary accommodation costs that cannot be recovered because Housing Benefit subsidy has been frozen since 2011
findings.detail: The Housing portfolio overspent by £2.263m driven by temporary accommodation and homelessness prevention. Housing Benefit subsidy rates were capped and frozen in 2011 and have not kept pace with rising temporary accommodation costs, creating a structural funding gap. The council housed 262 households in temporary accommodation during the year; despite efforts, 144 remained in temporary accommodation at year-end.
findings.matters: This is a recurring structural deficit the council cannot solve through its own actions. It results from a national subsidy rate that has not moved in 15 years while costs have risen, and it is explicitly identified as the primary driver of the council's overall overspend.
findings.figures: £2.263m Housing portfolio overspend; 262 households requiring temporary accommodation in 2025/26; 144 in temporary accommodation at year-end
findings.quote: Housing Benefit subsidy rules mean that the Council is unable to recover the full cost of temporary accommodation through Housing Benefit subsidy from the Department for Work and Pensions. Subsidy rates have been capped and frozen since 2011 and have not kept pace with the significant increase in temporary accommodation costs. As a result, a growing funding shortfall has arisen, with the associated financial pressure falling directly on the Council.

findings.paper_title: Report - Revenue, Capital and Prudential Indicators Outturn Reports 202526
findings.headline: £0.8m revenue overspend funded from reserves, 4% of the council's net revenue budget
findings.detail: The council's net revenue outturn was £20.4m against a revised budget of £19.6m. The overspend has been funded from the council's usable reserves. While the Section 151 Officer certifies this would not cause overall reserves to fall below prudent levels, it accelerates reserve depletion and signals financial stress.
findings.matters: Drawing down reserves to cover operational deficits indicates weakening financial resilience; the council's own S151 Officer explicitly states that reliance on reserves to fund recurrent deficits is not sustainable.
findings.figures: £0.8m overspend (4% of £19.6m revised budget); funded from Financial Management Reserve
findings.quote: The net revenue outturn was £20.4m compared to the revised budget of £19.6m, this has caused a £0.8m revenue overspend, which is 4% of the net revenue budget. The overspend has been funded from the Councils usable reserves.

findings.headline: Business Rates Resilience Reserve being built then held flat at £1.9m with no future receipts
findings.detail: The Business Rates Resilience Reserve grows from £538k to £687k in 2025/26, then to £1.937m by 2027/28. From 2027/28 onwards it receives no further in-year receipts (shown as zero) and remains static at £1.937m. This suggests the council will not be adding to the reserve after 2027/28 despite holding it for ongoing volatility risk.
findings.matters: A Business Rates Resilience Reserve reflects council concern about business rates income volatility. The fact it plateaus at a fixed level with no future growth suggests the council has calculated a minimum it can afford, beyond which operating budget pressure prevents further build-up.
findings.figures: Business Rates Resilience Reserve: £538k (opening), £687k (2025/26 close), £1,937k (2027/28 onwards)

findings.headline: Total usable reserves declining by 38% over six years from £33.8m to £20.9m
findings.detail: Overall usable reserves fall from £33.756m in 2025/26 to £20.88m by 2030/31. While some drawdown reflects planned capital spending (the CIL reserve falls from £13.7m to £1.3m), the sustained decline represents a significant reduction in the council's financial buffers.
findings.matters: A sustained, material decline in total reserves indicates either planned major capital investment (which needs explaining) or budget pressures being absorbed by reserve drawdown rather than operational change. Both matter to a lender assessing sustainability.

findings.headline: General Fund Balance declining to zero from 2026/27 and remaining there
findings.detail: The council's General Fund Balance, shown as £373k at 31 August 2025, is projected to decline through 2025/26 and reach £0 in 2026/27, remaining at zero thereafter. This is the council's buffer for unexpected costs or income shortfalls. A zero balance means no safety margin.
findings.matters: Lenders and finance directors assess financial resilience by the adequacy of emergency reserves. A General Fund Balance of zero signals minimal capacity to absorb unexpected costs or income volatility.
findings.figures: General Fund Balance: £373k (31/08/2025), £0k (2026/27 onwards)

findings.headline: Council acknowledges affordability pressures constraining borrowing decisions
findings.detail: The strategy explicitly references 'significant cuts to public expenditure and in particular to local government funding,' positioning affordability as a binding constraint on borrowing strategy. This language indicates the council faces budget pressures beyond routine variation and must weigh capital needs against the cost of debt.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether a council's borrowing decisions reflect genuine low-risk treasury management or are being driven by constrained affordability. Acknowledgment of funding cuts signals structural revenue pressures that could affect debt servicing capacity.
findings.figures: Authorised limit for borrowing: £25m; actual external borrowing: £2.7m (11% utilisation)
findings.quote: Given the significant cuts to public expenditure and in particular to local government funding, the Council's borrowing strategy continues to address the key issue of affordability without compromising the longer-term stability of the debt portfolio.

findings.headline: Investment portfolio shrinking to £12.6m; investment income at risk as reserves deploy
findings.detail: Net treasury investments are forecast to fall from £36.8m to £12.6m by 2029 as the council deploys cash to fund capital and revenue spending. Investment income is currently budgeted at £1.2m annually but will decline as the investment base shrinks. The council maintains a £10m liquidity buffer, leaving minimal margin above that threshold.
findings.matters: Declining investment balances reduce both financial flexibility and investment income available to support the budget. Once the council approaches the £10m liquidity floor, it loses the ability to smooth cash flow or manage unexpected pressures without external borrowing.
findings.figures: Net Investments: -£36,809k (31.03.25) → -£12,591k (31.03.29); Investment income budget 2026-27: £1.2m
findings.quote: Investments are due to fall as capital expenditure increases.

findings.headline: Capital programme growth funded entirely from reserve drawdown, not external borrowing
findings.detail: The Council's Capital Financing Requirement is increasing by £7.4m (37%) to fund a growing capital programme, but external borrowing is actually declining from £2.8m to £2.3m. The strategy continues to rely on internal borrowing and reserve depletion rather than accessing debt markets, despite explicitly noting that short-term interest rates are expected to fall, making external borrowing attractive.
findings.matters: A council with growing capital needs that avoids borrowing despite favourable rates may be credit-constrained or masking revenue pressures. The internal borrowing model—funding capital from reserves—is finite and unsustainable unless revenue improves.
findings.figures: General Fund CFR: £20,193k → £27,630k (+37%); External Borrowing: £2,829k → £2,321k (-18%)
findings.quote: The Council has an increasing CFR due to the capital programme.

findings.headline: Usable reserves declining 45% over five years despite growing capital programme
findings.detail: Usable reserves are forecast to fall from £38.3m in March 2025 to £21.0m by March 2029. Simultaneously, the Capital Financing Requirement is growing 37% (from £20.2m to £27.6m) due to expanding capital programmes. The strategy explicitly states that both 'capital reserves are used to finance capital expenditure and revenue reserves are used to finance the revenue budget.'
findings.matters: A council depleting reserves while capital spending grows signals either unsustainable funding practices or underlying revenue deficits. At current trajectory, discretionary reserves fall below £21m while capital needs are rising, reducing financial resilience.
findings.quote: Investments are due to fall as capital reserves are used to finance capital expenditure and revenue reserves are used to finance the revenue budget.

findings.paper_title: Budget 26-27 Report - Final Full Council Report
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation creates governance and financial planning uncertainty from April 2028
findings.detail: Havant Borough Council will cease to exist as a legal entity from April 2028, when the two-tier local government system is replaced by a unitary structure across Hampshire and the Isle of Wight. The council is transferring £1M from the Regeneration Capital Reserve to a new Local Government Reorganisation Reserve, and planning assumptions continue based on the current structure despite the imminent dissolution.
findings.matters: The planned dissolution introduces uncertainty around the continuity of council operations, debt liabilities, and financial commitments beyond 2028. Lenders need clarity on how debt and service obligations will be transferred to the new unitary authority.
findings.figures: £1M transfer to Local Government Reorganisation Reserve; dissolution date April 2028
findings.quote: from April 2028 it is expected that Havant Borough Council will no longer exist as a legal entity. However, the functions and responsibilities of the Council will continue, and financial planning should continue based on the known funding and demand pressure for the Council as it currently operates.

findings.paper_title: Budget 26-27 Report - Final Full Council Report
findings.headline: A cumulative £9.1M funding deficit is forecast across the medium-term financial strategy period
findings.detail: The MTFS forecasts funding gaps after transfers to reserves of £1.4M in 2027/28, £2.8M in 2028/29, £2.5M in 2029/30, and £2.4M in 2030/31, totalling £9.1M over four years. These gaps reflect ongoing service cost pressures (particularly housing and property), pay and non-pay inflation, reductions in income, and a limited resource base to absorb further increases.
findings.matters: A structural medium-term deficit requires sustained savings delivery to avoid further reserve depletion or emergency measures. The council's ability to close a £9.1M gap is critical to its financial sustainability.
findings.figures: £9.1M cumulative gap (2027/28–2030/31); individual years: £1.4M, £2.8M, £2.5M, £2.4M
findings.quote: These gaps reflect ongoing service cost pressures, particularly within housing and property services, alongside pay and non-pay inflation, reductions in income, and the Council's limited resource base to absorb further cost increases.

findings.paper_title: Budget 26-27 Report - Final Full Council Report
findings.headline: Reserves are falling below minimum prudent levels and represent a key financial risk
findings.detail: The council's usable reserves were 4.7% of net revenue budget at the start of the current year, predicted to fall to 2.1% by March 2026. Industry standards recommend a minimum of 5%. The 2026/27 budget includes a £436K transfer to reserves to rebuild, which would bring the level to 3.2% by March 2027—still significantly below the recommended minimum.
findings.matters: Reserve levels below prudent minimums indicate limited financial flexibility to absorb shocks or demand spikes, and are a core credit risk for lenders.
findings.figures: 4.7% (current), 2.1% (forecast March 2026), 3.2% (with transfer, March 2027), 5% (industry minimum recommendation)
findings.quote: Usable reserve levels remain low and continue to represent a key financial risk to the Council.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - Medium-Term Financial Strategy 2026-27 to 2030-31
findings.headline: Base budget subject to structural cost pressures (housing, inflation, service demand) expected to persist throughout the entire five-year period
findings.detail: Pressures from housing and property services, pay inflation, non-pay inflation, demographic demand, and income collection risk are all described as structural, implying they are not one-off or easily eliminated.
findings.matters: Structural pressures throughout the planning period indicate limited scope for cost reduction without service cuts, reducing financial flexibility and increasing risk of further deficits if savings targets are missed.
findings.figures: No single quantified amount; paper notes £1.1m for homelessness as example pressure requiring investment.
findings.quote: These pressures are structural in nature and are expected to persist throughout the MTFS period.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - Medium-Term Financial Strategy 2026-27 to 2030-31
findings.headline: Business rates transitional funding reduces over the period and ceases entirely from 2029/30, creating further income loss
findings.detail: The national business rates reset from 1 April 2026 reduces the proportion of rates retained by the council. Transitional funding was provided for the first three years but is designed to phase out, with no transitional funding assumed from 2029/30 onwards.
findings.matters: Loss of transitional support from 2029/30 will add to the funding pressure in a period when the council is already facing £2.4–£2.6m annual gaps and minimal reserves.
findings.figures: No quantified transitional funding amount disclosed for Havant.
findings.quote: The MTFS also recognises the implications of the national business rates reset effective from 1 April 2026, which will reduce the proportion of business rates retained by the Council. Transitional funding has been provided for the first three years to mitigate the impact, but this reduces over the period and is assumed to cease from 2029/30.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - Medium-Term Financial Strategy 2026-27 to 2030-31
findings.headline: Extended Producer Responsibility income of approximately £1.9m in 2026/27 is only confirmed until April 2028, creating a funding cliff
findings.detail: EPR funding depends on market activity and is confirmed only through 2027/28. The MTFS explicitly does not assume it beyond April 2028, meaning a £1.9m annual income loss from 2028/29 onwards unless replaced.
findings.matters: Loss of £1.9m annually coincides with the period when the budget gaps are largest (£3m+ in 2028/29), intensifying financial stress.
findings.figures: approximately £1.9m in 2026/27; assumed zero from April 2028.
findings.quote: While current forecasts indicate funding of approximately £1.9m in 2026/27, this income stream is dependent on market activity, is only confirmed until 2027/28, and is therefore not assumed beyond April 2028.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - Medium-Term Financial Strategy 2026-27 to 2030-31
findings.headline: Demand for temporary accommodation has increased significantly over past three years and continues to produce recurring budget overspends
findings.detail: Despite a £1.1m additional investment in 2026/27 to manage demand and prevent homelessness, the paper carries this pressure forward throughout the five-year period as a structural issue, implying the investment has not stemmed the underlying overspends.
findings.matters: Recurring overspends in a demand-led budget area that remains unresolved after targeted investment signals structural unaffordability and high risk of continued deficits.
findings.figures: £1.1m additional investment for 2026/27 onwards; no quantified spend or overspend size disclosed.
findings.quote: Demand for temporary accommodation has increased significantly over the past three years, leading to recurring budget overspends.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - Medium-Term Financial Strategy 2026-27 to 2030-31
findings.headline: General Fund reserves forecast to fall to 2.1% of Net Revenue Budget, well below the council's 5% minimum target
findings.detail: Reserves stood at 4.7% of NRB on 1 April 2025 and are forecast to fall to 2.1% by 31 March 2026, recovering only to 3.2% by March 2027—leaving the council 40–60% short of its own minimum threshold for three years.
findings.matters: Very low reserves severely limit the council's ability to absorb financial shocks, manage demand volatility, or bridge unexpected funding gaps. The paper itself notes reserves have fallen below best-practice guidelines.
findings.figures: 4.7% on 1 April 2025; 2.1% forecast 31 March 2026; 3.2% forecast 31 March 2027. Target: 5% of NRB.
findings.quote: the General Fund balance and Financial Resilience Reserve stood at 4.7% of NRB, forecast to fall to 2.1% by 31 March 2026, before improving to 3.2% by 31 March 2027.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - Medium-Term Financial Strategy 2026-27 to 2030-31
findings.headline: Forecast budget gaps of £671k–£3m in years 2–5, cumulative deficit of £9.2m by 2030/31
findings.detail: After a balanced 2026/27 budget, the MTFS projects adverse gaps of £671k in 2027/28, rising to £3.004m in 2028/29, then £2.552m and £2.396m in subsequent years. Cumulative unplanned deficit reaches £9.173m by 2030/31.
findings.matters: Substantial multi-year funding gaps indicate the council will need to identify additional savings, raise income, or draw on already-thin reserves—all constraints on creditworthiness.
findings.quote: These gaps represent the difference between forecast expenditure pressures and anticipated funding, after taking account of currently identified savings and approved growth.

findings.headline: Council has £34.5m commercial property investments generating 7.84% of net revenue stream
findings.detail: The council holds £34.5m in commercial property 'purely for financial gain' and depends on net income of £1.693m in 2026/27 to balance the revenue budget. This represents 7.84% of the council's total revenue funding - a material dependency on property market returns and tenant stability that creates exposure to economic downturn.
findings.matters: Heavy reliance on commercial property income for base-budget funding creates revenue vulnerability if property values fall, vacancy rates rise, or tenants default.
findings.figures: £34.5m total commercial investments; £1,693m net income forecast for 2026/27 (7.84% of net revenue stream)
findings.quote: With central government financial support for local public services declining, the Council previously invested in commercial property purely for financial gain. Total commercial investments are currently valued at £34.5m.

findings.headline: £3.9m of the 2026/27 capital programme is unfunded and will be financed by internal borrowing
findings.detail: Of £24.2m total planned capital expenditure, £3.9m (16%) has no identified external funding source and will be met by internal borrowing - drawing down cash reserves or incurring new debt. The council states: 'The Council is expected to fund all the unfunded schemes through internal borrowing.' This depletes liquidity and increases reliance on future cash generation.
findings.matters: A large unfunded capital programme indicates either optimistic revenue forecasting or insufficient capital discipline, and depletes the financial buffer needed for unexpected pressures.
findings.figures: £3,949m unfunded of £24,208m total capital expenditure in 2026/27 (16.3%)
findings.quote: The Council is expected to fund all the unfunded schemes through internal borrowing to avoid any additional finance costs.

findings.headline: Financing costs rising from 2% to 7% of revenue over three years as capital programme grows
findings.detail: The proportion of net revenue stream consumed by interest and minimum revenue provision (MRP) is forecast to rise from 2.05% in 2024/25 to 7.27% by 2028/29 - a 3.5× increase. Absolute financing costs climb from £0.373m to £1.731m. This accelerating charge reflects both the growing capital financing requirement (up 37% to £27.6m) and the council's reliance on debt-financed capital expenditure.
findings.matters: Rapidly growing financing charges squeeze operational budget headroom and reduce the council's capacity to absorb demand pressures or respond to service failures.
findings.quote: The revenue budget implications of expenditure incurred in the next few years will extend for up to 50 years into the future.

findings.headline: Community Infrastructure Levy receipts have collapsed from £3.2m to £307,000 annually
findings.detail: CIL receipts fell from £3.179m in 2021/22 to £828k in 2024/25 and are forecast at only £307k for 2025/26. The council explicitly states it cannot forecast when the housing market will recover and expects this to have 'short to medium-term impact on the provision of infrastructure.' This removal of a major capital funding source creates a structural funding gap.
findings.matters: Loss of developer contribution income forces the council to fund infrastructure from reserves or borrowing, reducing financial flexibility and increasing debt service costs.
findings.quote: We are faced with falling CIL receipts, consequent upon the wider economic climate impacting the housing market, causing fewer sites to be commenced. It is anticipated that gross CIL receipts for the financial year ending 31/3/26 will be in the region of £307,000.

findings.paper_title: 202425 Statement of Accounts, Audit Results Report and Auditors Annual Report
findings.headline: Control issues identified by auditors with council planning additional checks before accounts publication
findings.detail: EY identified control issues during the 2024/25 audit, with management responses detailed in the Audit Results Report. The council's finance team acknowledged that significant officer review is needed and stated that additional checks will be put in place to allow further review before the accounts are published.
findings.matters: Control issues flagged by auditors suggest the council's internal controls over financial reporting are not operating effectively, raising concerns about ongoing financial reporting accuracy and the council's ability to prevent and detect misstatements.
findings.figures: Control issues documented on pages 27-28 of Appendix B (Audit Results Report)
findings.quote: EY identified some control issues in year and management responses to these are noted on pages 27 and 28 in Appendix B. Significant officer review goes into the finalisation of the accounts and every effort is made to minimise any error. Additional checks will be put in place to allow further review before the accounts are published.

findings.paper_title: 202425 Statement of Accounts, Audit Results Report and Auditors Annual Report
findings.headline: Four uncorrected misstatements identified by auditors including valuation judgement differences of £3k net and Disabled Facilities Grants capitalisation issues
findings.detail: EY identified 4 uncorrected misstatements in the 2024/25 accounts. Two are judgemental differences relating to valuations between the council's third-party valuer and EY's valuation team, with a net effect of £3k. Two further projected misstatements were identified on the capitalisation of Disabled Facilities Grants expenditure and investment property income, though further review found no additional misstatements.
findings.matters: Uncorrected misstatements, even if judgemental, indicate the council's financial statements contain known inaccuracies that auditors were unable to resolve, suggesting control weaknesses in accounting and valuation procedures.
findings.figures: £3k net effect from judgemental valuation differences; 2 projected misstatements on DFG capitalisation and investment property income
findings.quote: There are 4 uncorrected misstatements identified by EY in the 2024/25 accounts as detailed on page 24 of Appendix B. There are 2 judgemental differences, and the net effect of these is £3k. These relate to differences in judgement on valuations between the third-party valuer the Council employs, and EY's valuation team.

findings.paper_title: 202425 Statement of Accounts, Audit Results Report and Auditors Annual Report
findings.headline: Disclaimed audit opinion for second consecutive year due to inability to assure opening balances and in-year movements
findings.detail: EY issued a disclaimed opinion on the 2024/25 accounts because auditors could not obtain sufficient assurance over opening balances and in-year movements, following a disclaimed opinion in 2023/24. The S151 officer attributes this to carry-over risks from the National Audit backlog and central government's backstop dates from 2022/23, noting that a disclaimer is worse than a qualified opinion. The council expects the disclaimer to continue through 2025/26 before moving to an unqualified opinion in 2026/27.
findings.matters: A disclaimed audit opinion means the council's financial statements cannot be fully relied upon for credit assessment, as auditors were unable to provide assurance on the accuracy of opening balances and in-year movements—a fundamental requirement for lenders evaluating creditworthiness.
findings.figures: Disclaimed opinions for 2023/24 and 2024/25; expected disclaimer for 2025/26, then unqualified opinion expected in 2026/27
findings.quote: A disclaimed audit opinion was issued in 2023/24 as no assurances could be given on the opening balances. As a result, a disclaimed audit opinion has also been issued for 2024/25 as audit have no assurance over in year movements and some closing balances.

findings.paper_title: Cabinet Report Savings and Efficiencies Programme 2026 27
findings.headline: Budget shortfalls anticipated beyond 2026/27 across the Medium-Term Financial Strategy period
findings.detail: The report references anticipated budget shortfalls over the full MTFS period (2026/27 to 2030/31), indicating the £1.54M deficit is only the start of a multi-year challenge.
findings.matters: Suggests the current deficit is structural, not one-off, and the council faces ongoing financial pressure that single-year savings may not resolve.
findings.quote: This report outlines the Council's strategic response to the projected £1.54 million budget deficit for 2026/27 and anticipated shortfalls over the Medium-Term Financial Strategy period.

findings.paper_title: Cabinet Report Savings and Efficiencies Programme 2026 27
findings.headline: Failure to deliver savings would force 'top slicing' or organisational restructure
findings.detail: The S151 Officer warns that if the formal savings programme is not approved and delivered, the council would need to resort to across-the-board budget cuts or major restructuring. This indicates the savings programme is the managed alternative to crisis measures.
findings.matters: Signals what happens if the planned savings do not materialise; suggests significant service disruption risk if delivery fails.
findings.figures: £1.54 million deficit
findings.quote: Failure to approve a dedicated savings and efficiency programme would result in more drastic measures being required to balance the 2026/27 budget. These could include "top slicing" of budgets, or an organisational wide restructure.

findings.paper_title: Cabinet Report Savings and Efficiencies Programme 2026 27
findings.headline: £1.7M savings programme identified, including discontinuation of non-statutory services
findings.detail: The council has developed a £1.7M savings plan to close the gap, delivered through service redesigns, income generation, and review of non-statutory functions. This includes increases to fees, charges, and parking revenues.
findings.matters: Lenders need to assess whether the council has a credible, funded plan to return to balance or whether further deterioration is likely.
findings.figures: £1.7M in savings and efficiencies
findings.quote: The outcome of this process has identified £1.7M in savings and efficiencies which includes an increase in fees and charges and a review of parking charges across the borough.

findings.paper_title: Cabinet Report Savings and Efficiencies Programme 2026 27
findings.headline: £1.54 million budget deficit for 2026/27 cannot be funded from depleted reserves
findings.detail: The Council's reserves have been drawn down by overspends in recent years and cannot cover the projected deficit. The S151 Officer states explicitly that a funded savings programme is essential because reserves are no longer available as a buffer.
findings.matters: A council that cannot use reserves to manage a deficit must cut spending or raise income; it has no flexibility. Reserve depletion is a sign of structural budget stress.
findings.figures: £1.54 million, Financial Resilience Reserve
findings.quote: The Council's reserves have also diminished as overspends in recent years have required funding from the Financial Resilience Reserve. This means that the assumed budget deficit for 2026/27 cannot be funded from reserves and a clear plan to reduce expenditure and/or increase income is required.

findings.headline: Treasury management non-compliance recurred in 2024/25 when day-to-day cash management exceeded the council's individual counterparty limit.
findings.detail: The council exceeded its own treasury management counterparty limit in its day-to-day bank account during 2024/25, repeating the same breach from 2023/24. Mitigation measures were implemented (opening additional treasury bank accounts and investing in money market funds), but the non-compliance recurred at lower levels. The underlying cause is identified as the large sums of council tax deposited on behalf of precepting authorities, creating cash management pressures.
findings.matters: A lender assessing credit risk would want to understand why the council repeatedly breaches its own treasury management policy on routine operations despite implementing controls, and whether this signals inadequate operational capacity.
findings.figures: Specific breach amounts not provided in the main report text
findings.quote: There has been one non-compliance of our own treasury management limits due to the management of cash in our day-to-day bank account exceeding the individual counterparty limit.

news_drafts.headline: Capital Financing Requirement forecast to rise 31% from £21.7m to £28.4m by 2029; council shifting to net borrower status
news_drafts.lead: Material increase in planned capital spending and borrowing requirements signals a shift in council's financial strategy; affects debt sustainability, refinancing requirements, and medium-term funding dependency.

news_drafts.headline: £8m short-term loans borrowed at year-end to support cash flow; represents 75% of total borrowing
news_drafts.lead: Substantial reliance on short-term borrowing for cash management indicates underlying revenue/expenditure timing mismatches; creates refinancing risk and dependence on short-term market conditions.

news_drafts.headline: Usable reserves fell by £4.7m to £33.6m; working capital down £6.7m amid volatile cash flows
news_drafts.lead: Declining reserves and tight working capital reduce financial flexibility. The wide swing in investment balances (£29m range) indicates the council operates with compressed cash buffers and requires careful cash flow management.
